Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Public Transport: Bus riding, Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem

Vignette:
Ravi was twenty-five years old, a counselor at a community mental health center in a mid-sized city, and she had built her life around the belief that people could heal. That belief had been straightforward until eleven months ago, when she was pulled over on her way home from a late shift. The officer’s voice had been flat, almost bored, as he ordered her out of the car. She had done everything right—hands visible, movements slow—but within seconds she was on the ground, her cheek pressed into the asphalt, a knee grinding into her lower back. The smell of damp soil and exhaust fumes filled her nose. She remembered the weight of the officer’s body, the way her own arms were twisted behind her, the cold metal of the handcuffs biting into her wrists. She had not resisted. She had not even spoken. And yet, for what felt like an eternity, she was certain she was going to die.

In the weeks that followed, Ravi tried to return to her normal routines. She took the bus to work because her car had been impounded and she could not afford the towing fees. But every time the bus lurched to a stop, her body would lock into the same position she had been in on the ground—shoulders hunched, arms pinned behind her back, breath shallow. She would feel the pressure of the knee again, even though nothing was touching her. Sometimes the memory came back as a full sensory flood: the taste of grit, the distant sound of traffic, the weight of the officer’s radio pressing into her ribs. Other times she could recount the entire event to herself and feel nothing at all, as though it had happened to a stranger she had once known. That numbness frightened her more than the reliving did, because it made her wonder if she had already become someone else.

She began to avoid the people she had socialized with before the event. They were kind, well-meaning, but she could not shake the feeling that they were not what they seemed. She studied their faces during conversations, searching for the flicker of something dangerous beneath the surface. Her body would react before her mind caught up—a sudden freeze when a colleague touched her shoulder, a racing heart when a client mentioned an encounter with police. At home, she could not fall asleep without checking the mirrors in her apartment three or four times, making sure no one had entered through a window she had already locked. She covered her face with her hands when she walked past a police car, as though that would make her invisible.

The worst part, she told herself, was the feeling of contamination. She showered twice a day, sometimes three times, but the sensation of that pavement against her skin never fully washed away. She had come to believe that she had lost her connection to her community and her culture, that the event had severed something essential. She was a counselor who no longer trusted people, who flinched at the smell of soil after rain, who could not ride a bus without her body reenacting the moment of her own powerlessness. Her supervisor had noticed her arriving late, her eyes darting, her hands trembling during team meetings. When she finally told her supervisor that she needed help, Ravi was not sure whether she was hoping to be fixed or simply to be believed. What frightened her most was the possibility that the numbness would win—that one day she would recall what happened and feel nothing at all, and that would be the moment she stopped being the person she had always tried to be.
